info.no_code_html: Don't have an access code? Write to me at angel.lamenor@gmail.com.
info.why_p1: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) starts from a simple idea: there is no single student and no single way of learning. That is why it proposes offering different ways of representing information, different ways of acting on and expressing what has been learned, and several paths to engage and stay motivated. Above all, it aims to anticipate barriers instead of waiting for them to appear.
info.why_p2: The problem comes when you take it into the classroom. UDL shows where to go, but not how to turn its principles into specific decisions when writing the instructions of an activity. It asks, for example, to avoid information overload, but it doesn't say where the limit is. So two teachers with the same principles can reach very different solutions. Checklists and rubrics help review an activity that is already done, but not build it. And if you ask an AI to apply UDL, it reproduces the same ambiguity: the same task, two different answers.
info.why_p3: LEdui (Lectura Educativa Inclusiva, Inclusive Educational Reading) was created to bring UDL down to earth. Its principles become ten rules that say what to look at, what to change and why in the instructions of a task. To make them concrete, LEdui also draws on other standards: Easy Reading (UNE 153101:2018 EX), with criteria for writing and structuring understandable texts; the WCAG web accessibility guidelines; and the UNE 71362:2020 standard for the quality of digital educational materials. The goal was not to create another theoretical framework, but to have a concrete guide for everyday use, so that the task stops being an obstacle and the student can focus on what they really need to learn.
info.rules_intro: These are the ten LEdui rules. The application you can try here is based on them and puts them into practice with artificial intelligence algorithms that aim for a deterministic response model, so that the result depends on the rules rather than on each moment's interpretation.
info.r1_text: Short sentences, active voice and everyday vocabulary. If a technical term is needed, it is kept and explained in brackets.
info.r2_text: Numbered steps in order, separating the essential from the secondary.
info.r3_text: Introduction, development and close, with connectors that link the ideas.
info.r4_text: Friendly and encouraging. Effort is valued and mistakes are treated as part of learning.
info.r5_text: Hints, clarifications and examples so the student can move forward without help.
info.r6_text: The objectives are kept and made explicit, with submission criteria and an estimated time.
info.r7_text: Teamwork or peer assessment when it makes sense.
info.r8_text: An open question that invites students to think and relate what they've learned to their own experience.
info.r9_text: Examples from work or everyday life.
info.r10_text: For example, a document, a presentation, a video or audio.
info.bio1: Computer engineer from the University of Castilla-La Mancha. Before teaching, he spent ten years in the educational publishing sector as a team lead at publishers and edtech companies such as Pearson and ODILO, and has taken part in educational publishing organisations such as ANELE and IPA.
info.bio2: He now teaches Computing in Vocational Training at CIFP Virgen de Gracia in Puertollano (Ciudad Real, Spain), where he works with community-impact projects, artificial intelligence and educational radio, with a special focus on inclusive education and open educational resources.
info.award1: Top 50, Global Teacher Prize 2025 (unofficially known as the “Nobel Prize of Education”).
info.award2: 2nd Teacher in the World, Muallem Prize 2026 of the Bourham Foundation.
info.tfg_html: LEdui was developed as a Bachelor's Final Project (Trabajo Fin de Grado) for the Degree in Computer Engineering at the University of Castilla-La Mancha, supervised by Carlos González Morcillo.

info.cta_title: Do you have an idea where LEdui could help?
info.cta_text: If you have an educational project and think LEdui could be useful, write to me. I'd love to hear your idea and see how we can work together.
info.rules_img_alt: Diagram: LEdui at the centre of four standards: UDL, WCAG guidelines, Easy Reading (UNE 153101:2018) and UNE 71362:2020.
info.needs_p1: Taken together, the rules address five groups of needs. Rules 1, 2 and 3 (clarity, structure and coherence) are the core of the standard and support dyslexia and other specific learning difficulties. Rule 2 also supports autistic students, because it anticipates what comes next, avoids information overload and keeps a predictable sequence, and students with ADHD, because it separates the essential from the secondary and fits each step into a single span of attention. Intellectual disability is covered by simplified language, clear structure and rule 5, which offers hints and examples in place of the teacher's help. Rules 4 and 8 address emotional regulation and frustration: they value effort, anticipate difficulties, present mistakes as part of the process and ask open questions with no single right answer.
